analysis.one_liner: Ends tax breaks that reward companies for shifting profits and jobs offshore.
analysis.headline: The bill has 140 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, but has not moved past a committee referral since February 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make U.S. multinational companies pay regular U.S. tax on profits their foreign subsidiaries earn each year, instead of the reduced rate they pay now, and would stop companies from lowering their U.S. tax bill by blending profits from high-tax and low-tax countries together. It would also tax foreign-based companies that are run from the United States as if they were domestic companies, and crack down on "corporate inversions," where a U.S. company reorganizes abroad on paper while keeping most of its business here [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. taxpayers generally, because the bill would raise more revenue from multinationals that now shift profits to low-tax countries [S2]. Domestic workers benefit indirectly, because current law gives companies a lower effective tax rate on income booked offshore than on income earned here, which tilts decisions toward locating profits and activity abroad [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Taxes the offshore profits of U.S. multinationals each year at ordinary rates by repealing the current reduced rate and deduction, removing the discount companies get for booking income abroad
Requires country-by-country calculation of foreign tax credits, so companies can no longer use taxes paid in high-tax countries to shield profits parked in tax havens
Limits interest deductions for domestic companies in large international groups, curbing a common technique of loading U.S. companies with debt to shrink their taxable U.S. income
Tightens rules on corporate inversions, treating foreign reincorporations with 80% or more U.S. ownership, or with management and control primarily in the U.S., as domestic companies for tax purposes
Treats foreign corporations managed and controlled in the United States as domestic corporations for income tax, closing the gap for companies that operate here but are chartered abroad
Closes a specific oil-industry shelter by taxing foreign base company oil related income currently rather than deferring it

analysis.who_pays: U.S. multinational corporations that currently pay little or reduced U.S. tax on profits booked through foreign subsidiaries, and their shareholders, who would see lower after-tax returns as the bill taxes those profits at ordinary rates and narrows deductions and credits [S2].

drawbacks.text: Raising the effective tax rate on foreign earnings could make U.S.-based multinationals less competitive against foreign rivals and, critics argue, could push investment and even headquarters overseas rather than bringing profits home

The country-by-country rules, interest-deduction limits, and managed-and-controlled test would require complex new regulations and add compliance costs for companies operating in many countries, costs that could partly reach consumers
The bill raises revenue but does not direct it to any specific purpose, so any benefit to ordinary taxpayers depends entirely on what Congress later does with the money

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets well-documented loopholes — profit shifting to tax havens, debt-loading of U.S. subsidiaries, and paper inversions — and its costs fall mainly on multinational shareholders rather than on wages directly. The strongest good-faith objections are competitiveness and complexity: taxing foreign earnings at full U.S. rates without the current deduction could put U.S. companies at a disadvantage against foreign rivals and encourage real relocation, and the country-by-country machinery would be complex to administer. On balance the reforms address practices that cost the treasury revenue and tilt decisions against domestic workers, but the bill's real-world value depends on the revenue being used well and on the anti-avoidance regulations being written carefully.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sits in the House Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it since it was referred in February 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 5, 2025 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means
It has 140 cosponsors, all of them Democrats
No committee action, markup, or floor vote has occurred since the referral

The bill would tax foreign subsidiary profits currently, apply the foreign tax credit country by country, repeal the reduced rate and deduction for foreign and foreign-derived income, limit interest deductions for multinational groups, tighten inversion rules, and treat foreign corporations managed and controlled in the United States as domestic

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations and their shareholders are better off for now, because the current tax rules the bill would change remain in place while the bill sits without committee action.

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 140 House cosponsors for it

for.name: House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill shortly after introduction

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a markup or any further action on the bill since it was referred on February 5, 2025

sides.party_line_note: All 140 cosponsors are Democrats, no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-chaired Ways and Means Committee has taken no action since the February 2025 referral.

industries.industry: U.S. multinational corporations with offshore profits, especially tech and pharmaceutical firms
industries.note: The bill taxes their foreign subsidiary profits in the year earned at full U.S. rates instead of the reduced current rate, applies the foreign tax credit country by country so low-tax-haven profits can no longer be sheltered by high-tax-country credits, and limits interest deductions for large multinational groups.

The bill adds a new category of 'foreign base company oil related income' taxed as immediate Subpart F income unless the oil was extracted and sold within the producing country, directly hitting arrangements that route oil sales through low-tax affiliates.

industries.industry: Foreign-incorporated but U.S.-managed companies and inversion deal structures
industries.note: The bill would treat foreign corporations whose management and control is primarily in the United States as domestic for income tax purposes, and treats post-2017 inverted companies as domestic when 80% or more of the stock is held by former U.S. owners or management stays in the U.S.

analysis.trajectory: Bills like this that sit in the House Ways and Means Committee without a markup rarely reach the floor, and with no Republican cosponsors and Republican control of the committee and the House, the most likely path is that the bill stays parked and dies at the end of the 119th Congress, as earlier versions of the same proposal did in prior Congresses.
